units.current: You grew up level with the people around you.

You treat your family as equals, present and practical and never fussy. Because closeness when you were small came from standing side by side, you show tenderness late and mostly through what you do. You turn up to fix a family problem before anyone asks, and you rarely say what you feel while you do it.

In your first home a sibling or a cousin stood beside you as an equal, and the two of you looked after each other. You learned to settle things between yourselves, and the adults were the last to hear about them.
You grow from trusting yourself first.

Every skill you have began with deciding that you could do it. Because you learned early to depend on yourself, nobody can push you into learning, and you take to a teacher only once you have chosen them. You pick things up faster with one other person learning beside you, and you let few people that close.

You taught yourself things as a child that the adults around you had not shown you, and you kept quiet about how hard it was. By the time you were grown you had a stubborn way of learning, on your own terms and at your own pace.
You grew up sharing everything with family.

You treat family as people with a natural claim on your time, your space and your money. Because sharing was how your first home held together, refusing a relative feels like disloyalty to you. You give without fuss, and you resent it quietly when the giving is taken for granted.

The money and the clothes and the space were all shared in your first home, and a sibling or cousin was never far from what was yours. Growing up you gave without being asked, and you could tell exactly who had taken what.
You give money easily and keep track of it.

You lend to family before you have finished saving for yourself, and you rarely ask for it back. Because money at home was always pooled, a private account feels slightly selfish to you. Your savings grow slowly while your family's claims stay open, and you feel both generous and short.

You saw money borrowed and lent around the family as a child, and little of it was written down. Before you were grown you had given away more than you could spare, and you had learned which relatives paid you back.
Your family holds together across distance.

You keep close ties with relatives who live far away, and you are the one who calls first. Because distance was ordinary when you were growing up, a long absence never feels to you like a break in love. You are the link between relatives who would otherwise lose touch.

In your first home people spoke of a relative who had moved away, or you moved yourself and made friends quickly in each new place. By the time you were grown your family stretched across more than one place, and you felt at home in each of them.
Your chances with money grow the further you go.

You find your best chances away from home, in a new city or an unfamiliar market or among strangers. Because familiar places feel small to you, you look outward for money before you look nearby. You earn far from home and feel safe only once the money is back in one place.

Money in your family came through moving when you were young, a relative working away or a business that travelled. The first money you made yourself came from beyond your own neighbourhood, and you liked how that felt.
You were loved at home in an unusual way.

You show love to your family through ideas and help with problems more than through surface warmth. Because the care you got early was quiet and odd, you trust a relative who understands you more than one who fusses over you, and you feel lonely at noisy gatherings. You come home as the quiet one, and your relatives have stopped trying to change that.

In your first home someone gave you books, questions or long silences in place of the usual fuss, an adult who lived in their own head. By your teens you had learned to answer your own questions, and you asked for help less than other children did.
You taught yourself most of what you know.

You learn best alone, from books and odd sources and your own testing, at a pace no class has ever matched. Because nobody handed you a set path, you trust the understanding you dig out yourself, and you forget what you were simply told. You know a great deal that you have never shown anyone.

Whatever you were given to read when you were small, you read past it into subjects nobody around you shared. By your teens you knew more about a few odd things than most adults did, and you mentioned it only to the one or two people who asked.
Your growth comes through the unusual teacher.

You grow fastest through unusual people and unplanned turns, the odd teacher or the subject you stumbled on. Because the standard routes never fitted how you learn, you find them dull and leave them early. You grow in your own order, and others notice only when it is done.

A person outside the usual line taught you most as a child, a neighbour or relative with odd interests who took you seriously. By your teens you had grown in ways your family could not quite follow, and you had stopped expecting them to.
You carried more at home than anyone knew.

At home you protect your family closely, and you take on their problems before they ask. Because you learned early to carry weight without help, you find it hard to let anyone see you struggle. Your family relies on your strength, and few of them know what it cost you to build.

notes.issue: The last sentence of How you are has no "you" as its subject, against the voice law.
notes.fix: "At home you protect your family closely, and you take on their problems before they ask. Because you learned early to carry weight without help, you find it hard to let anyone see you struggle. Your family relies on your strength, and you have told few of them what it cost you to build."

units.current: In your first home you carried a weight few people saw, a strict rule or a hard stretch or a worry beyond your age. By your teens you were the steady one in your family, and you kept your own needs to yourself.
Hard years are the ones that grow you.

You grow when life is hard, and you lose direction when it gets too comfortable. Because difficulty was where you first found your strength, you sign up for the harder option by choice, and a year with nothing hard in it leaves you restless. You have done your best learning in seasons other people would call their worst.
Each hard year of your childhood left you more capable than the one before, at school or at home or in a sport. You came to trust difficulty more than ease, and by your teens you went looking for it.
Your body is strong and holds its strain.

Your body has deep reserves, and it keeps going long after most people would stop. Because you learned as a child to hide how tired you were, you notice exhaustion late, and it shows in short sleep and a short temper. You recover well once you finally rest, and you rarely rest early enough.

You were a tough child, slow to complain and quick to hide a bad night from the adults. Your reserves got you through hard weeks most children did not have to face, and you learned early to run on them.
Your family gets your honesty along with your love.

You love your family most easily where you are allowed to disagree, and a home that asks you to keep quiet feels cold to you. Because honesty was your first way of belonging at home, you say what others leave unsaid, and a relative or two finds you hard work. Your warmth is real, and you show it most to the people who argue back.

You questioned at least one rule in your first home that everyone else accepted, quietly or out loud. Someone there found you difficult for it, and by your teens you had learned which opinions to keep to yourself.
You grow by doubting what you are given.

You improve anything you are handed by questioning it first, a method or a belief or a piece of advice. Since accepting things whole has never felt honest to you, you learn more slowly from teachers and faster from your own mistakes. Your doubt turns into skill whenever it has real work in front of it, and you grow restless when it has none.

You had outgrown some of what your family believed by your teens, and you got there by arguing with it. In school you did best in the subjects that let you question the answer, and you drifted through the ones that did not.
You were fed well, and you became the one who feeds.

You hold your family together through comfort, the visit kept and the favour done and the table set. Because care reached you first as warmth, you give it back the same way, and you feel useless in a family crisis that kindness cannot touch. What you want from your family is ease, and you work hard to make it.

Someone in your early life, an older relative who gave without being asked, made comfort a daily thing. You still judge a home by how it feels to walk into, and you have made yours warmer than the ones you grew up beside.
Your body trusts food and rest to put it right.

You trust your body to fix itself with a good meal and a long sleep, and for most of your life it has. Because comfort is how you recover, you reach for it under stress, and you turn the extra helping or the lost weekend into a habit before you notice. Your body asks you for rhythm more than for effort.

You were a child who recovered quickly, from colds and falls and bad days alike. Your appetite and your sleep were steady, and you came into adulthood with more reserve than most of the people around you.
Your family pays back what it is given, and so do you.

You rely on your family more than on friends, because help between you has come back each time it was needed. Since your first home kept careful accounts, you keep track of what is owed between relatives without saying so. You give help readily, and you feel uneasy until a debt is settled.
As a child you knew that money at home was handled carefully and that nothing was spent without a reason. Early on you counted your own money and kept your word the way the household did.

notes.issue: Keeping your word is the Magistrate's force here ("relied on your word", "keeping your word is how you feel at peace"). On D153 the line sits beside the Magistrate's "relied on your word". 子平真诠 论财 against 论正官.
notes.fix: "As a child you knew that money at home was handled carefully and that nothing was spent without a reason. Early on you counted your own money and saved it the way the household did."

units.current: Your money grows quietly from early habits.

You save without thinking about it, a little from everything, and spending without a reason feels wrong to you. Because careful habits were normal in your first home, you build wealth slowly and steadily, and few people notice until it is large. You enjoy keeping money more than spending it, and a big purchase stays on your mind for weeks.

You kept coins and small earnings longer than your friends did as a child, and nobody had to tell you to. You learned early that money kept quietly was money that stayed, and you have never lost the habit.
You absorbed your family's rules early.

The expectations you grew up with stay with you, and you feel uneasy when a family duty goes undone. Because approval at home came through doing things right, you check yourself against what your elders would think. Your bond with your family is strong and dutiful, and you feel its pull wherever you live.

You knew the rules of your first home without being told, and you rarely needed correcting. By your teens you had taken on an older relative's standards as your own, and you held yourself to them strictly.
You grow best inside a clear structure.

You grow by finishing what you start, the course completed and the level passed and the standard met. Because structure is where you first felt secure, you do well wherever the steps are clear and lose heart when they are not. Your progress is steady, and you climb further than people who started faster.

Your school years ended with a record of steady progress, each year finished well and responsibilities taken on early. Teachers and older relatives trusted you, and you came to measure your growth by the steps you completed.
You were truly looked after as a child.

In family life you expect warmth, and you give it back without thinking. Because care at home was steady from the start, you trust your relatives easily and find it hard to believe the worst of them. You take it harder than most when a relative lets you down, because you never expected it.

A parent or an older relative looked after you closely when you were small, and you came to rely on their calm. By your teens you expected the world to treat you with the same care, and mostly it did.
You grow best from a safe base.

You take your biggest steps from a secure position, with people behind you and a home to return to. Because safety came first in your life, you learn faster when you feel held, and you stall under pressure from people you do not trust. You put off a change until the support is in place.

As a child you tried new things when someone you trusted stood close by, and you held back when nobody did. By your teens you were slower than your friends to try things away from home, because home felt so safe.
Your body recovers best when someone looks after you.

You get your energy back quickly after tiring weeks and bad nights, and faster still when someone close is fussing over you. Because care was what restored you from the start, you let yourself rest properly only when another person insists. Your body does well on trust, rest and good company.

Whenever you were tired or run down as a child, someone was there with a meal and an early night, and you were yourself again within days. By your teens you had a steady energy the adults around you counted on, and you have kept much of it since.
